To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the pursuit of community self-sufficency is a primary motivation for First Nations communities in engaging with community energy projects and that the pursuit of self-determination, in particular, has implications for how community energy is viewed, planned, implemented, and assessed.

remote and off-grid communities have a desire for self-sufficiency that is both material and political in nature and that this desire is incongruent with current approaches to energy policy and technology development in these communities.

community energy projects are often motivated by a desire for self-sufficiency, that this desire has two dimensions, and that it is somewhat incongruous with the approach to community energy projects taken in British Columbia.

how remote communities might be better served in the pursuit of their energy projects and how the pursuit of these projects might better serve communities.

the implications of this pursuit on community energy projects in remote First Nations communities and how it might inform the way that community energy policy and technology development is approached.
the implications of the pursuit of self-determination in community energy projects and the ways in which this goal might be reconciled with the goals of government and industry.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pursuit of self-determination and decolonisation through community energy projects in remote and First Nations contexts is not well served by current community energy policies and approaches.

the pursuit of community self-sufficience in the context of remote community energy projects is a complicated process of balancing material and political goals, and that it requires the involvement and support of government and industry to achieve.

the pursuit of self-determination and self-sufficiency among remote First Nations in British Columbia is not well supported by existing approaches and policy mechanisms, and that a new approach is necessary to support these communities in their energy pursuits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the pursuit of community self-sufficency in the form of energy self-sufficiency is not a simple matter of implementing renewable energy technologies, but rather one that requires a fundamental rethinking of community and energy development processes.
the communities we have studied are not looking for a handout, but are rather looking to develop the capacity and resources to become more self-sufficient.
remote First Nations communities are pursuing energy projects that are not necessarily about the pursuit of sustainability, but about the pursuit of self-determination.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the pursuit of self-determination and self-sufficiency among First Nations communities in BC is an important factor that must be accounted for in the development of community energy projects in these communities and that the pursuit of these goals is somewhat incongruous with the current policy and technological approaches that are being taken to address energy needs of remote and First Nations in Canada.

the pursuit of self-determination and self-sufficiency among First Nations communities in BC should be a central concern in the development of community energy projects and the policies that support them.

community energy projects are not simply about providing a community with a new technology or a new source of energy, but rather they are about a community's desire to be self-sufficient and to be in charge of the energy decisions that are made on their behalf.
